program: Travel English -- Europe Without a Translator
hub_subtitle: Travel English for the airport, the check-in counter, the hotel and passport control — so that Europe needs no translator

lesson.menu_title: What Do You Think? -- Recommending a Place
lesson.menu_desc: A breakfast room in Florence, a young couple with a guidebook, and the question she never expected to hear in English: "You know Italy -- what do you recommend?" After seventeen lessons of asking, this is the lesson where she answers. The grammar: turning an opinion into advice -- I'd recommend going early, it's worth taking the boat, if I were you, I'd stay two nights, it's too crowded / it isn't big enough. New words for places: a must-see, charming, breathtaking, lively, a highlight, overrated, touristy, pricey, to skip, disappointing -- 39 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- What Do You Think?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosângela | Lesson 18 -- What Do You Think?
lesson.grammar_point: recommendation and evaluation structures (I'd recommend + -ing, it's worth + -ing, If I were you I'd + base verb, too + adjective / not + adjective + enough)

listenings.text: My name is Bruno, and for thirty years I have driven the same road along this coast, the narrow one, with the sea on your left and the rock on your right. Every passenger who sits behind me asks me the same question, sooner or later: what should we see? And for the first ten years I gave them a list. Ten places, twelve places, everything in the book. Then I understood something. A list is not an answer. A good answer is one opinion and one reason, and nothing more. I would rather tell you one thing that is worth your morning than ten things you will forget before lunch. So here is mine. The famous beach, the one on every postcard, the one everybody photographs: it is a little overrated. In August it is too crowded, the sand is not big enough for the people who are standing on it, and you will spend two hours in a line to sit in somebody else's shadow. Honestly? I would skip it. Take the early boat instead, at eight, before the water gets busy, and look at this coast from the sea. That is the way it was built to be seen. And one more thing, from thirty years of driving. Some people arrive with the guidebook open and they leave with the guidebook closed, and every single thing they did was in it. Their trip was fine. But it was somebody else's trip. The passengers who come back to me years later, who remember my name, are always the ones who took one honest recommendation from a real person. Nobody has ever told me they remember a guidebook. They remember a stranger at breakfast who said: if I were you, I would go here.

I am Diane, I am seventy years old, and for most of my life every place I visited was nice. That was my word. The cathedral was nice. The dinner was nice. Venice, Prague, Seville: all of them nice. I saw so much more than I could ever say, and because I had only that one word, I sounded like a woman with no opinions at all. People stopped asking me about my trips, and I understood why. Nobody wants to hear that everything was nice. And then, two years ago, in a small hotel in Seville, a young couple sat down at the table next to mine with a map, and the girl turned to me and asked where they should eat that night. I almost said it. I almost said everything here is nice. But I stopped, and I tried. I said the restaurants on the square were pricey, and a bit touristy, and that if I were them, I would walk two streets behind the church and eat where the local families eat, and go late, because nobody in Spain eats at seven. Six or seven sentences. My hands were cold the whole time. The next morning they came to my table before I had finished my coffee, and they told me it was the best dinner of their trip. And I sat there, seventy years old, with my heart going fast, because something had changed. That was the day I stopped being a tourist that somebody helps, and became a traveler that somebody asks. It did not take perfect grammar. It took an opinion, and one reason, and the courage to say it out loud.

structure.title: Four ways to turn what you think into advice
cards: The safest, warmest way to recommend anything. After recommend, the verb wears -ing: "I'd recommend going in May." "I'd recommend taking the boat." You can also put a noun there: "I'd recommend the small restaurant behind the church." Never "I recommend to go".
is it worth the time or the money?

This one answers the real question: is it worth my morning? "It's worth taking the boat, even for one day." And the negative saves people a whole afternoon: "It's not worth waiting two hours for that line." After worth, the verb wears -ing too, exactly like after enjoy and after used for.
If I were you, I'd + plain verb

The kindest frame of all, because you are not telling somebody what to do: you are putting yourself in their shoes. "If I were you, I'd stay two nights." Two rules: it is always were, for every person, and after I'd the verb is plain, with no to. Never "if I was you", never "I'd to stay".

Too means more than you want: "In August it's too crowded." Enough means the right amount: "In May the sea is warm enough to swim." And not enough means less than you need: "One day isn't long enough for Florence." Watch the order: too goes in FRONT of the adjective, enough goes AFTER it.

paras: It is a quiet May morning in Florence, and Rosângela is alone at a breakfast table with her second coffee, her husband still upstairs. At the next table there is a young couple from Canada, Daniel and Emma, with a guidebook open between the plates and a small argument going on across it: the coast tomorrow, one day, and forty things in the book. Then Daniel turns around in his chair and says: "Excuse me — you know Italy, don't you? What do you recommend?" And for one whole second Rosângela looks behind her, because in four years of traveling nobody in Europe has ever asked her a question that started with those three words: what do you.

Then she puts the cup down and answers. "I'd recommend starting early — the road gets busy after ten. The little town on the hill is charming, much nicer than the big one." Daniel points at the famous beach, the number one thing in the book. "Honestly? I'd skip it. It's a bit overrated, and in summer it's too crowded — the sand isn't big enough for everybody." She tells them it is worth taking the boat, because the view from the water is breathtaking and it was the highlight of her own trip. She tells them the restaurants on the square are pricey and rather touristy, and that if she were them, she would have dinner two streets away. Ten minutes, maybe twelve. And the whole time, Emma is writing it down — not in the guidebook, in her own notebook.

Here is what Daniel and Emma will never know. Four years ago, in a coffee shop in Paris, Rosângela was the one at that table with the book open, waiting for her son to order for her, because she could not do it herself. She was the one who asked, always, and somebody was always answering. And nothing about this morning needed perfect grammar — nobody at that table was listening for her tenses. Advice is not grammar. Advice is one opinion and one reason, said out loud by somebody who was actually there. That is all it has ever been, in any language. And this morning, for the first time, the person who was actually there was her.

gist.prompt: Which sentence says best what the text is about?
choices: A guide to the best places on the Italian coast in May.
Two Canadian tourists who cannot decide what to do with one free day.
The morning a traveler who always asked for help became the person somebody else asks for advice.

items: Daniel asks Rosângela for a recommendation because he thinks she knows Italy.
True. He turns around and says: "you know Italy, don't you? What do you recommend?" — the first time in four years of traveling that anybody in Europe has asked her that.
Rosângela recommends the famous beach from the guidebook.
False. She says she would skip it: it is a bit overrated, and in summer it is too crowded — the sand isn't big enough for everybody. She recommends the boat instead.
She says the view from the water was the highlight of her own trip.
True. She tells them it is worth taking the boat, because the view from the water is breathtaking, and it was the highlight of her trip.
Emma writes the advice in the guidebook, next to the beach.
False. Emma writes it down in her own notebook, not in the guidebook — the whole ten or twelve minutes.
The text says her English had to be perfect for the couple to trust her advice.
False. Nobody at that table was listening for her tenses. The text says advice is not grammar: it is one opinion and one reason, said out loud by somebody who was actually there.

items.situation: A traveler at the next table asks when is the best month to visit the coast. Answer, and give a reason.
tips: I'd recommend going in May. In August it's too crowded.
May or September. In summer it's too hot, and the towns are too full.

items.situation: They have one free afternoon and ask what is worth doing. Recommend one thing.
tips: It's worth taking the boat. The view from the water is breathtaking.
It's worth walking up to the old town. It's charming, and much quieter.

items.situation: They are planning one single day in Florence. Give them personal advice.
tips: If I were you, I'd stay two nights. One day isn't long enough.
If I were you, I'd sleep here and go to the coast the next morning.

items.situation: They want to have dinner on the main square. Tell them honestly what you think.
tips: Honestly? The restaurants on the square are pricey and a bit touristy.
It's not worth eating there. I'd walk two streets and eat with the families.

items.situation: They ask about the famous beach everybody photographs. Be honest, and be kind.
tips: It's a little overrated, to be honest. I'd skip it.
Everybody goes, but it's too crowded in summer and the sand isn't big enough.

items.situation: They ask what the best part of your last trip was.
tips: The boat to the islands was the highlight of the whole week.
The small square at night. It's very lively, with music until eleven.

items.situation: They ask if the famous restaurant in the book is any good. It was not.
tips: It was disappointing, honestly. Slow, and not very good.
We went, and it wasn't worth the money. It's not worth booking.

items.situation: You have given them your advice, and you want the conversation to continue. Ask them something.
tips: And you? What did you like best so far?
How long are you staying? Where do you go after Italy?
